title: Which are sources of light?
stem:
Athe Sun
Bthe Moon
Ca lit candle
Da mirror

Which of the above are sources of light?
key: A source of light gives off its own light. The Moon and mirrors only reflect light.

options.text: A, B and C only
options.pick: The Moon shines brightly at night, so it seems to make its own light.
options.why: The Moon reflects light from the Sun. It gives off no light of its own.

options.text: A and C only
options.pick: Ask of each one: does it give off its own light?
options.why: The Sun and a lit candle give off their own light. The Moon and a mirror only reflect light.

options.text: A, B, C and D
options.pick: All four look bright, so they all seem to be sources.
options.why: Looking bright is not enough. The Moon and a mirror only reflect light from a source.

options.text: A and B only
options.pick: The Sun and the Moon are both lights in the sky.
options.why: Only the Sun gives off its own light. A lit candle does too, so it is a source.

title: A book in a dark room
stem:
Ali is in a room with no light at all. He cannot see the book on the table.

Why?
key: An object that is not a light source is seen only when it reflects light from a source into our eyes.

options.text: The light from his eyes is too weak to reach the book.
options.pick: It feels as if we look out at things, so sight seems to go out from the eyes.
options.why: Light does not come out of our eyes. It must travel from the object into the eyes.

options.text: The book is not a source of light, so it can never be seen.
options.pick: Only things that give off light seem to be visible in the dark.
options.why: Books are seen all the time: when there is light, they reflect it into our eyes. In the dark there is none to reflect.

options.text: The darkness blocks the light coming from the book.
options.pick: Darkness seems to be something that gets in the way.
options.why: Darkness is just the absence of light. The book has no light to reflect in the first place.

options.text: No light reaches the book, so none is reflected into his eyes.
options.pick: Ask where the light that lets him see the book would come from.
options.why: A book is seen only when it reflects light from a source into the eyes. With no light, nothing is reflected.

title: Seeing the Moon
stem: We can see the Moon at night because…
key: The Moon is not a source of light. It reflects light from the Sun into our eyes.

options.text: it reflects light from the Sun into our eyes.
options.pick: The Moon is not a source of light. Where does its light come from?
options.why: Sunlight falls on the Moon and is reflected to the Earth, into our eyes.

options.text: it gives off its own light.
options.pick: The Moon glows brightly, like a lamp.
options.why: The Moon gives off no light of its own. It reflects the Sun's light.

options.text: light from our eyes lights it up.
options.pick: We look at the Moon, so our eyes seem to reach out to it.
options.why: Light does not come out of our eyes. Light from the Moon must enter our eyes.

options.text: it is a source of light at night, but not in the day.
options.pick: The Moon seems to shine only at night.
options.why: The Moon is never a source of light. It always reflects light from the Sun; at night it simply stands out against the dark sky.

title: Three cards with holes
stem:
Siti looks through holes in three cards, P, Q and R, and sees a candle flame. Card Q is then moved a little to one side, and she can no longer see the flame.

Why?
key: Light travels in straight lines. It reaches the eye only along a straight path through all three holes.

options.text: The light bends around card Q but cannot bend back into the next hole.
options.pick: Light seems able to curve a little around things.
options.why: Light does not bend around the card. It travels in straight lines, so card Q simply blocks it.

options.text: The light still reaches her eye, but card Q makes it too dark to see.
options.pick: The flame is still burning, so its light seems to be getting through.
options.why: If light from the flame entered her eye, she would see it. Card Q blocks the light, so none enters her eye.

options.text: Light travels in straight lines, and the holes are no longer in a straight line.
options.pick: Picture the path of the light from the flame to her eye.
options.why: Light can reach her eye only along a straight line through all three holes. Moving Q puts card in the way.

options.text: Light can pass through card Q only when it is in the middle.
options.pick: The candle was visible when Q was in the middle.
options.why: Light never passes through the card itself. It passes through the hole only when the hole is in line with the others.

title: Tracing paper in front of a torch
stem:
A torch shines on a sheet of tracing paper held in front of a screen. Tracing paper lets some light through.

Which describes the shadow on the screen?
key: Partly blocking the light makes a lighter shadow. The shadow is always on the side away from the light.

options.text: No shadow, because light passes through the paper
options.pick: Light gets through, so there seems to be nothing to make a shadow.
options.why: Only some light gets through. The rest is blocked, so a lighter shadow forms.

options.text: A dark shadow, the same as a book's
options.pick: Any object in the way seems to make the same shadow.
options.why: A book lets no light through and makes a dark shadow. The paper lets some through, so its shadow is lighter.

options.text: A shadow on the torch side of the paper
options.pick: The shadow seems to belong near the light.
options.why: A shadow always forms on the side of the object away from the light.

options.text: A lighter shadow, because the paper blocks only some of the light
options.pick: The paper partly blocks the light. What does partial blocking give?
options.why: Some light still reaches the screen behind the paper, so the shadow is lighter than one from a book.

title: Moving the screen
stem:
Wei moved the screen further and further from an object. The torch and the object did not move. His results are shown.

What can he conclude?
figure:
Distance between object and screen (cm)Height of shadow (cm)
106
209
3012
key: With the torch and object still, the further the screen is from the object, the bigger the shadow.

options.text: The further the screen is from the object, the smaller the shadow.
options.pick: Moving things apart seems to make them look smaller.
options.why: The table shows the opposite: the shadow is biggest when the screen is furthest away.

options.text: The further the screen is from the object, the bigger the shadow.
options.pick: Read the table in one direction: as the distance goes up, what does the shadow do?
options.why: From 10 cm to 30 cm, the shadow grows from 6 cm to 12 cm.

options.text: The size of the shadow depends only on the size of the object.
options.pick: The object decides the shadow's shape, so it seems to decide its size too.
options.why: The object did not change, yet the shadow changed. The screen's distance made the difference.

options.text: He cannot conclude anything, because the object did not move.
options.pick: An experiment seems to need the object to move.
options.why: He meant to change the screen's distance and keep everything else the same. That is a fair test.

title: Turning a plate
stem:
A round plate is held between a torch and a screen, with its flat face towards the torch. Its shadow is a circle. The plate is then turned so that its edge faces the torch.

What shape is the shadow now?
key: A shadow has the outline of the object as seen from the light.

options.text: Still a circle, because the plate is round
options.pick: The plate has not changed, so its shadow seems not to change.
options.why: The shadow has the outline the light sees. Edge-on, that outline is a thin bar, not a circle.

options.text: No shadow, because the plate is too thin to block the light
options.pick: A thin edge does not seem to block anything.
options.why: The edge still blocks a strip of light, so there is a thin shadow.

options.text: A thin bar
options.pick: Picture the plate as the torch sees it once it is edge-on.
options.why: Edge-on, the plate blocks only a thin strip of light, so the shadow is a thin bar.

options.text: A bigger circle
options.pick: Turning the plate seems to spread its shadow out.
options.why: Turning the plate edge-on makes it block less light, and the shadow becomes a thin bar.

title: A fair test on screen distance
stem:
Mei wants to find out how the distance between an object and the screen affects the size of the object's shadow.

Which plan is a fair test?
key: Change only the variable being tested. Keep everything else, including the other distance, the same.

text: the distance between the object and the screen
the object, the torch, and the distance between the torch and the object
options.pick: Change only the distance being asked about; keep everything else the same.
options.why: Any change in the shadow can then come only from the object-to-screen distance.

text: the distance between the object and the screen, and the distance between the torch and the object
options.pick: Moving both distances seems to give more results.
options.why: Two things change at once, so she cannot tell which one changed the shadow.

text: the distances between the torch, the object and the screen
options.pick: Changing the object will certainly change the shadow.
options.why: That tests the size of the object, not the screen distance.

text: the distance between the torch and the object
the distance between the object and the screen
options.pick: It is a distance, so it seems to fit the question.
options.why: That tests the torch-to-object distance, which is a different variable.

title: Seeing around a corner
stem:
Bala uses two mirrors to see an umbrella around a corner.

Which explains how he sees it?
key: Mirrors give off no light. They reflect light from the object on, into the eyes.

options.text: Light from his eyes travels to the mirrors and then to the umbrella.
options.pick: He is looking into the mirrors, so his sight seems to travel out.
options.why: Light travels from the umbrella into his eyes, not the other way.

options.text: Light from the umbrella is reflected by the two mirrors into his eyes.
options.pick: Follow the light from the umbrella to Bala's eyes.
options.why: Each mirror reflects the light on, so light from the umbrella reaches his eyes even though it is not in a straight line from him.

options.text: The mirrors give off light that shows him the umbrella.
options.pick: Mirrors look bright, so they seem to make light.
options.why: Mirrors give off no light of their own. They only reflect light.

options.text: Light bends around the corner to reach his eyes.
options.pick: The light does get around the corner somehow.
options.why: Light travels in straight lines. The mirrors change its direction by reflecting it.

title: Not a source
stem: Which of these is not a source of light?
key: A source gives off its own light. The Moon only reflects the Sun's light.

options.text: A firefly
options.pick: An insect does not seem like something that makes light.
options.why: A firefly gives off its own light, so it is a source.

options.text: Lightning
options.pick: Lightning is weather, not an object.
options.why: Lightning gives off its own light, so it is a natural source.

options.text: A lit candle
options.pick: A candle is just wax and a string.
options.why: When it is lit, its flame gives off light, so it is a source.

options.text: The Moon
options.pick: Which of these only reflects light?
options.why: The Moon reflects light from the Sun and gives off none of its own.

title: A mirror in the dark
stem:
Ahmad looks into a mirror in a completely dark room.

What does he see?
key: A mirror only reflects light. In complete darkness there is no light to reflect.

options.text: Nothing, because no light reaches the mirror to be reflected
options.pick: A mirror only reflects light. Is there any light to reflect?
options.why: With no light at all, the mirror has nothing to reflect into his eyes.

options.text: His face, because a mirror gives off light
options.pick: Mirrors always seem bright.
options.why: A mirror gives off no light of its own. It only reflects light.

options.text: His face, because light from his eyes is reflected back to him
options.pick: When he looks into a mirror, he sees his own eyes looking back.
options.why: Light does not come out of our eyes. Without a light source, there is nothing to reflect.

options.text: A faint picture, because mirrors store some light
options.pick: Shiny things seem to keep a little glow.
options.why: Mirrors do not store light. In the dark there is no light to reflect.

title: Seeing an apple
stem: How does Lina see a red apple on a table in a sunny room?
key: Light travels from the object into the eyes. The apple reflects sunlight.

options.text: Light from her eyes travels to the apple.
options.pick: She points her eyes at the apple, so her sight seems to go out.
options.why: Light travels from the apple into her eyes, not the other way.

options.text: The apple gives off red light.
options.pick: The apple looks bright red, as if it glows.
options.why: The apple gives off no light of its own. It reflects sunlight.

options.text: The apple reflects light from the Sun into her eyes.
options.pick: The apple is not a source of light. Where does the light that reaches her eyes come from?
options.why: Sunlight falls on the apple, and the apple reflects some of it into her eyes.

options.text: Sunlight enters her eyes, and her eyes then find the apple.
options.pick: The room is bright, so her eyes seem ready to see anything.
options.why: To see the apple, light must come from the apple into her eyes. That happens because the apple reflects sunlight.

title: The darkest shadow
stem: Which of these objects of the same size makes the darkest shadow?
key: The more light an object blocks, the darker its shadow.

options.text: A sheet of frosted glass, which lets some light through
options.pick: Frosted glass looks cloudy, so it seems to block a lot.
options.why: Some light still passes through, so its shadow is lighter.

options.text: A sheet of clear plastic, which lets most light through
options.pick: Plastic is solid, so it seems to make a solid shadow.
options.why: Most light passes through, so it makes almost no shadow.

options.text: They all make equally dark shadows, because they are the same size.
options.pick: Same size seems to mean same shadow.
options.why: How dark a shadow is depends on how much light the object blocks, not only on its size.

options.text: A wooden board, which lets no light through
options.pick: The more light an object blocks, the darker its shadow.
options.why: The board blocks all the light, so its shadow gets no light at all.

title: Three objects, three shadows
stem:
A book, a sheet of tracing paper and a sheet of clear glass, all the same size, are held in front of a torch one at a time.

Which describes their shadows?
key: No light through: dark shadow. Some light through: lighter. Most light through: almost none.

options.text: All three shadows are the same, because the objects are the same size.
options.pick: Size seems to decide the shadow.
options.why: Size decides how big the shadow is. How dark it is depends on how much light gets through.

options.text: Book: dark. Tracing paper: lighter. Glass: almost none.
options.pick: Rank them by how much light each one lets through.
options.why: The book lets no light through, the paper some, and the glass most.

options.text: The glass makes the darkest shadow, because glass is the thickest.
options.pick: A thicker sheet seems to block more.
options.why: Clear glass lets most light through, so it makes almost no shadow.

options.text: The tracing paper makes no shadow, because light passes through it.
options.pick: Some light gets through, so there seems to be no shadow.
options.why: Only some light gets through. The rest is blocked, so there is a lighter shadow.

title: A cone pointing at the torch
stem:
A cone is held with its pointed tip facing a torch.

What shape is its shadow?
key: The shadow's shape is the outline of the object as the light sees it.

options.text: A triangle, because a cone looks like a triangle from the side
options.pick: Cones are usually drawn as triangles.
options.why: That is its side view. The torch sees it tip-on, and from there its outline is a circle.

options.text: A small dot, because only the tip faces the torch
options.pick: Only the point seems to be in the way.
options.why: The whole cone is behind the tip, and its round base blocks a circle of light.

options.text: A circle
options.pick: Picture the cone as the torch sees it, tip first.
options.why: Seen from the torch, the cone's outline is its round base, so the shadow is a circle.

options.text: The shape cannot be known without turning the cone.
options.pick: It seems you need to see it from several sides.
options.why: The shadow's shape is the outline the torch sees right now: a circle.

title: Which object?
stem:
An object's shadow is a rectangle when the torch shines on its side, and a circle when the torch shines on its end.

What could the object be?
key: Match each shadow to the object's outline from that direction.

options.text: A can
options.pick: Find a shape that is round at its ends and rectangular from the side.
options.why: A can is a cylinder: a rectangle from the side, a circle from the end.

options.text: A ball
options.pick: A ball is round, which fits the circle.
options.why: A ball makes a circle from every side, never a rectangle.

options.text: A book
options.pick: A book fits the rectangle.
options.why: A book makes a rectangle from every side, never a circle.

options.text: A cone
options.pick: A cone has a round end, which fits the circle.
options.why: From the side, a cone makes a triangle, not a rectangle.

title: Screen moved closer
stem:
A toy and a torch stay still. The screen is moved closer to the toy.

What happens to the shadow?
key: With the torch and object still, a screen closer to the object gives a smaller shadow.

options.text: It becomes bigger, because the screen is closer.
options.pick: Things look bigger when you get closer to them.
options.why: The shadow is not looked at from closer. It spreads less before reaching the screen, so it is smaller.

options.text: It becomes smaller.
options.pick: The shadow spreads out as it travels further. What happens if it travels less far?
options.why: With the screen closer to the toy, the blocked light has less distance to spread, so the shadow is smaller.

options.text: It stays the same size, because the toy has not changed.
options.pick: The toy is the same, so its shadow seems the same.
options.why: The screen's distance also changes the shadow's size.

options.text: It becomes bigger, because the toy is now nearer the torch.
options.pick: Nearer the torch does make a bigger shadow.
options.why: The toy did not move, so it is no nearer the torch. Only the screen moved closer.

title: Reading the results
stem:
The torch and a toy did not move. The screen was moved, and the height of the toy's shadow was measured.

Which change made the shadow smaller?
figure:
Distance between toy and screen (cm)Height of shadow (cm)
4012
3010
208
key: Read the table in one direction: as the screen comes closer, the shadow shrinks.

options.text: Moving the screen further from the toy
options.pick: Moving away seems to make things smaller.
options.why: The furthest screen (40 cm) gave the biggest shadow.

options.text: Changing the size of the toy
options.pick: A smaller toy would make a smaller shadow.
options.why: The toy was not changed. Only the screen moved.

options.text: Moving the screen made no difference.
options.pick: The toy and torch stayed still, so the shadow seems fixed.
options.why: The table shows the shadow changing from 12 cm to 8 cm as the screen moved.

options.text: Moving the screen closer to the toy
options.pick: Follow the table: as the distance shrinks, what happens to the shadow?
options.why: The shadow fell from 12 cm to 8 cm as the screen came from 40 cm to 20 cm.
